records.name: Gracijonas
records.facts_used: Gracijonas: The dictionary of written Lithuanian by Alfred Senn and Antanas Salys lists Gracijonas as a personal name and pairs it with Latin Gratianus. Gratianus was a Roman name derived from Latin gratus, “grateful”. The Lithuanian form adapts this Latin name with the masculine ending -as; the dictionary does not say when or by which route it entered Lithuanian use. The entry appears in the fifth volume of the Senn–Salys dictionary, published in Heidelberg in 1968, and was reprinted photographically in Salys’s collected writings in 1983. Behind the Name notes an early bearer, Saint Gratian, the first bishop of Tours in the fourth century. The dictionary entry records the spelling and its Latin equivalent, not the first Lithuanian bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Senn–Salys, Wörterbuch der litauischen Schriftsprache vol. 5 (Heidelberg 1968), proper-name list reprinted photographically in Salys 1983, PDF p. 232 / printed p. 217: original page image read at 250 dpi as 'Gracijõnas, -o s. m. /2/ PN Gratianus' (accent mark on o). Reprint note PDF p. 201 identifies the source and year. BTN Gratianus = Latin form of Gratian; Gratian from Roman name Gratianus < Latin gratus 'grateful'; Saint Gratian first bishop of Tours (4th century). The 1964 calendar (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 304) prints 'Gacijonas (Gacys)' on 18 December, a different spelling not used as evidence. Entry route into Lithuanian use and first bearer are not documented.

records.name: Neeme
records.facts_used: Neeme: According to Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966), Neeme is a name of literary origin that was presented as ancient. Rajandi considers it probably an intentional or accidental variant of Meeme, the name of an elder mentioned in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, and doubts any link with the documentary name Nemo. The Meeme connection is his qualified assessment, not a recorded line of transmission. Rajandi traces the name to M. Morrisson’s story about the Estonian struggles for freedom, published in Tartu in 1902, whose title hero is Neeme. According to him, Neeme came into use at the beginning of the twentieth century and, though never frequent, still held a share of about two to three names per thousand in the 1960s. This dates the literary model, not the first registered bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Rajandi 1966, PDF pp. 132–133 / printed pp. 134–135 (page image checked): Neeme is a literary name offered as ancient, from M. Morrisson's story 'Eesti-rahwa vabaduse võitluste üle' (Tartu 1902), whose title hero is Neeme; probably an intentional or accidental variant of Meeme, an elder named in Henry's Chronicle of Livonia; link with documentary Nemo doubted; came into use early 20th century, about 2–3 per mille; variants Neemi and Neemo. The Meeme step is Rajandi's 'tõenäoselt' (probably) and stays qualified in the text. The 1902 story itself was not opened; the date is Rajandi's.

records.name: Mairo
records.facts_used: Mairo: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) treats Mairo as a masculine counterpart of Maire, a feminine name borrowed from Finnish. records.name: Artemijs
records.facts_used: Artemijs: The name corresponds to Russian Артемий, which the Latvian Language Agency’s Russian rendering guide (Grabis and Porīte, 1993) renders as Artemijs. Russian Артемий continues Greek Artemios, a name derived from that of the goddess Artemis. Siliņš’s Latvian dictionary links the name with Greek artemēs, “unharmed, safe”, while Behind the Name describes the goddess’s own name as of unknown, possibly pre-Greek origin. The deeper root therefore remains open. Siliņš’s dictionary gives 1825 as the earliest known written attestation of Artemijs and 1851 as its earliest calendar entry. These are the earliest dates listed in that dictionary, not proof of the first bearer in Latvia. The 1993 rendering record documents the standard spelling, not the beginning of the name’s use.

records.name: Toom
records.facts_used: Toom: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) lists Toom, together with Tomm and Tommi, as a short form of Toomas, the Estonian form of Thomas, a name explained as Aramaic for “twin”. He adds that Toom can also be a short form of Dominikus and Chrysostomus. Julius Mägiste had compared Toom with Toomas only with a question mark in 1929, so the double source of the short form should be kept in mind. According to Rajandi, the name Thomas spread widely among Estonians from the fifteenth century. St Thomas’s Day on 21 December, the same date as the name day of Toom, had a place in the folk calendar with many customs and beliefs. These dates concern the Toomas family and the feast, not the first bearer of the short form Toom.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Rajandi 1966, PDF p. 162 / printed p. 164, Thomas article: Toomas usual, but short forms Tomm(i) and Toom also occur (Toom is also a short form of Dominikus and Krisostomus); Aramaic 'twin'; spread among Estonians from the 15th century; Toomapäev (21 December) had a role in the folk calendar with customs and beliefs. PDF p. 165 index: Toom → Thomas. Mägiste 1929 PDF p. 50 / printed p. 48 question-marked comparison (reused, earlier round) is superseded by Rajandi's explicit statement but mentioned. Dates are family/feast-level and labelled as such.

records.name: Tommi
records.facts_used: Tommi: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) lists Tomm and Tommi among the short forms of Toomas, the Estonian form of Thomas, a name explained as Aramaic for “twin”. Rajandi notes that St Thomas’s Day, 21 December, had a place in the Estonian folk calendar with its own customs and beliefs; Tommi’s name day falls on the same date. records.name: Vambo
records.facts_used: Vambo: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966), citing Andrus Saareste’s conceptual dictionary of 1959, lists Vambo as an alternative form of Vambola. Vambola itself is a literary name created by Andres Saal for his story of 1889. Rajandi suggests that Saal drew on the war chief Wamba in Kreutzwald’s Lembitu and on a Walter Scott character called Vambo, and possibly on the place name Varbola; these are proposed models, not one proven source. Rajandi records Vambo in the register of the Nõmme civil registry office for 1957. The full form Vambola appears as a given name in Tartu church books in 1905. The two dates belong to different spellings, and neither is necessarily the first use.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Rajandi 1966 PDF p. 221 / printed p. 223 (page image checked): 'Vambo ehk Vambola ← AS; Nm 57'. Abbreviations: AS = Andrus Saareste, Eesti keele mõisteline sõnaraamat, Stockholm 1959 (PDF p. 230); Nm 57 = Nõmme civil registry office 1957 (PDF p. 239). PDF p. 173 / printed p. 175, Vambola article: purely literary name; Andres Saal's 'Vambola' (1889) drew on Kreutzwald's 'Lembitu' war chief Wamba and a Walter Scott character name Vambo; model may also be sought in the place name Varbola; Vambola as a given name in Tartu church books 1905. Leole (reused) supports the short-form relationship. Varbola and vambas remain unproven models.

records.name: Senni
records.facts_used: Senni: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) describes Senni as a short form of several base names: Eugenia, also in Karelian use; Johanna, through English Jenny; and Ksenia in Estonian pronunciation. Under Eugenia he adds that the Russian short form Zhenya appears both in Karelia and in Estonia as an independent name in the form Senni. Which line applies depends on the bearer’s own full name or family tradition. Rajandi’s 1966 book records Senni as a name in independent use in Estonia. Because it is a short form of several names, it has no single date of origin, and the book does not give the first Senni registration.

records.name: Iivi
records.facts_used: Iivi: Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) places Iivi among the long-vowel variants of the Ive, Ivi and Ivika name group. He notes that some forms of this group were dialect variants of Eva in earlier centuries, while Julius Mägiste presented the commonest form, Ivi, in 1929 as an artificially created name. Iivi therefore belongs to this group, but its exact route is not settled, and Rajandi warns that names grouped this way may differ in origin. Rajandi records Iivi, alongside Hivi and Hiivi, as a less frequent variant in use in the 1960s, when Ivi was the preferred form. Mägiste’s 1929 date refers to Ivi, not to Iivi, and the book gives no first registration for Iivi.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Rajandi 1966 PDF p. 83 / printed p. 85 (page image checked): '*Ive ~ Ivi ~ (Iva ~) ~ Ivika ja teisendid pika algusvokaaliga moodustavad praegu ühtse nimerühma, mille mõned kujud Eva variantidena on olnud murdeliselt rahvapruugis juba möödunud sajandeil; levinuima teisendi Ivi esitas J. Mägiste 1929. a. «kunstlikult loodud» nimena ... Esineb ka variante Hivi, Iivi ja Hiivi.' Preface PDF p. 8 warns that short- and long-vowel names grouped together may be of different origin. Exact Iivi listed; route (Eva dialect form vs. Mägiste coinage) explicitly unsettled. Mägiste 1929 date belongs to Ivi.

records.name: Evelin
records.facts_used: Evelin: Behind the Name treats Evelin as the German, Estonian and Hungarian form of Evelina, which it explains as a Latinate form of the Norman name Aveline. Edgar Rajandi’s Estonian name book (1966) instead lists Evelina and Evelyn, pronounced Evelin, among the derived forms of Eva. Both connect the Estonian name with the Evelina and Evelyn forms, but they differ on its ultimate root. Rajandi counted the Eva group among 4,000 girls’ names given in Tartu in 1930–1942: Evelin occurred four times. Among people who changed their names in 1935–1940, six women gave up the name Evelin. These figures describe one city’s records, not the first Estonian Evelin.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: BTN Evelin (curated): German, Estonian and Hungarian form of Evelina. BTN Evelina: Latinate form of Aveline (Norman French form of Germanic Avelina, diminutive of Avila); some regard it as a variant of Evelyn or extension of Eve. Rajandi 1966, PDF p. 58 / printed p. 60 (page image checked): Eva article lists the derived form Evelina ~ Evelyn(e) [Evelin]; Tartu 1930–42, 4,000 girls' names: Evelin 4; among name changers 1935–40, 6 Evelins gave up the name. The two root explanations (Aveline vs. Eva) are kept explicit. ERR News 17 April 2015 (Evelin Ilves) was opened but not used.

records.name: Genė
records.facts_used: Genė: The dictionary of written Lithuanian by Alfred Senn and Antanas Salys (1968) marks Genė as a short form of two full names, Eugenija and Genovaitė. Eugenija is the feminine form of Eugenius, whereas the same dictionary matches Genovaitė with German Genoveva. Genė therefore has no single source name: the full name of each bearer determines which line applies. The name calendar in Stasys Yla’s book Tikiu Dievą (Chicago, 1964), whose short forms were reviewed by Salys, shows the same double link. It gives Genė in parentheses after Genovaitė on 3 January and after Eugenija on 25 December. The calendar records recommended short forms, not the first use of Genė.
records.reason: Exact-form scholarly bridge and a dated record, both opened and checked on the original page, support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining root uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Senn–Salys 1968 list, Salys 1983 PDF p. 230 / printed p. 215, original image read: 'Gẽnė, -ės s. f. /2/ KF von Eugènija und Genovaitė' (KF = short form). PDF p. 231 / printed p. 216: 'Genovaitė PN Genoveva'. The Yla/Salys calendar (Tikiu Dievą, Chicago 1964; reprint PDF p. 300 footnote; short forms reviewed by Salys) gives Genovaitė (Genė) on 3 January (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 286) and Eugenija (Genė) on 25 December (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 304). BTN Eugenia: feminine of Eugenius. The earlier comparison 'Eugenija / Genovaitė' is now documented as a double short-form relationship; no single source name is selected.
